title: Weight-loss drugs: appetite, fat absorption and energy use
ariaLabel: Schematic of weight control: appetite signals in the brain, fat absorbed from the gut, and energy use. GLP-1 agonists reduce appetite and slow stomach emptying, sympathomimetic drugs such as phentermine reduce appetite through noradrenaline, and orlistat blocks fat digestion in the gut.
caption: Schematic, not to scale. Flow and levels are qualitative and illustrative; no dose, concentration or lipid value is shown or implied.
blockInfo: A drug of the chosen class acting at this step (generic teaching symbol, not a named drug's shape). Less passes here, with the effects shown at the cholesterol and the LDL receptors.

nodes.label: Appetite signals
nodes.info: Hunger and fullness signals in the hypothalamus.

nodes.label: Weight gain
nodes.info: A teaching score for the energy balance that drives weight gain. It does not show how much weight any drug will take off.

edges.label: appetite centres
edges.info: GLP-1 agonists (semaglutide, liraglutide) act on appetite centres, slow stomach emptying and raise insulin when glucose is high. Sympathomimetics (phentermine) act through noradrenaline release.

edges.label: fat digestion
edges.info: Orlistat blocks gastric and pancreatic lipase, so about a third of dietary fat is not absorbed. It causes oily stools and can lower absorption of fat-soluble vitamins.
More fat absorbed raises weight gain.

sources: Where each class acts. GLP-1 agonists reduce appetite, phentermine reduces appetite through noradrenaline, and orlistat blocks fat digestion. This is standard teaching in the pharmacology texts the PrepNucleus lessons cite (Katzung; KD Tripathi) and were not checked against a linked source here, so they are flagged for review.
simplified: Diet, exercise and surgery, naltrexone with bupropion, setmelanotide, safety (pancreatitis, gallstones, heart valve disease with older drugs), expected weight loss, regain on stopping and eligibility are left out. Weight gain is drawn as a teaching score. Levels and the size of each effect are illustrative. The drug choices are teaching toggles of a class: no named drug, dose or schedule is shown or implied, and the figure does not say who should or should not take any of them.
